"This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
Another top general has been fired, the latest of more than two dozen senior military officials
pushed out by the Trump administration, NPR's Quill Lawrence reports President Trump didn't
seem to know who the general is.
Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia served for 32 years, including combat, and was in
a key planning job for the Joint Chiefs until he was suddenly fired.
The Pentagon is investigating the general for allegedly leaking information to the press.
When asked about it, President Trump seemed not to know exactly who, or at least what
gender, the general is.
"She's got problems, she's going to have big problems, she did.
Well, very much looking for leakers."
General Sylvia and his son have been the target of right-wing influencer Laura Loomer.
The Pentagon press secretary, without naming the general, said this matter and others have
been referred to the Justice Department.
Quill Lawrence, NPR News.
President Trump continued to criticize Brazil's election.
A day after the loser in the race, Flavio Bolsonaro and his family fled to the U.S.
Today, Trump declined to say whether he recognizes incumbent Luis Inacio Lula da Silva as president.
I don't want to comment it right now, but I thought the election was a very great embarrassment
to the people of Brazil.
I watched the election.
I didn't take sides.
I let it be.
I was asked not to take sides by the president, the current president.
Bolsonaro is facing charges of corruption and money laundering.
His father, Jair Bolsonaro, is in prison for attempting a coup after he lost the 2022 election.
The flu has shown up in the South and West, but other parts of the country have yet to
see many cases, from member station WYPR Scott Massione has more.
Early indicators show that current cases of the flu are driven by a variant of the H1N1
virus.
Michigan's University immunology researcher Andrew Pachach says that this year's vaccine
has good coverage for what the nation has seen so far.
Right now, there is no cause for concern, but this should be viewed as a good last call
to get your influenza vaccination for this year.
This year's the first year that the mRNA vaccine is available, which uses a synthetic
strain of genetic material instead of a killed form of the virus.
Researchers say they're watching closely to see how the new vaccine stacks up to the
traditional form.
If it performs well, it could offer a faster rollout for vaccines against unexpected flu
variants.
For NPR News, I'm Scott Massione in Baltimore.
The economy grew at a healthy 3.4 percent annual pace from July through September, driven
by consumer spending and AI investment.
But not everybody's feeling the benefit, as NPR's Stephen Besaha explains.
One of the first things I heard was disbelief that was from Jeannie Kimberley.
Kimberley says herself and her neighbors are all scraping to get by, and she just doesn't
buy these economic numbers.
There just continues to be a disconnect between what the numbers are showing us and how people
are feeling about them.
Part of the problem is that inflation is still high.
Prices rose 3.6 percent in September, according to a reading on inflation we got today.
NPR's Stephen Besaha reporting.
This is NPR News from Washington.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is amplifying claims that the country's election
earlier this week was stolen by Arab-led parties; final results confirm that Netanyahu's block
has lost its majority in parliament.
The opposition accuses Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population after a strong showing
by Arab-led parties.
If the opposition teams up with those parties, they could form the next government.
Netanyahu's Likud Party targeted Arab-led parties even before the vote, despite lacking
specific evidence.
A new study finds that some birds experience jet lag, and Piers Jeff Brumfield has more
on why.
The main shearwater lives in the British Isles.
When birds mate, one partner will sit on the egg and incubate it non-stop whilst the other
one goes out to sea.
Patrick Lewin of Oxford University led this new study, which appears in the journal Science.
After two weeks hunting at sea, the shearwater heads home as fast as it can.
It flies using the sun, but to use the sun as a compass, you have to know what time of
day it is.
In other words, your internal clock must be synced.
Changing time zones can mess that up, and GPS data showed the shearwater veered off
course on the way home, though only by a little.
"It's a really small addition."
Still, it's scientific evidence that even birds can get scrambled by a long flight.
Jeff Brumfield, NPR News.
Milwaukee could come to a standstill tomorrow as fans celebrate the Brewers' first World
Series title.
Fans will close, and thousands of fans are expected to line the streets for a victory
parade.
The small market brewers clinched the title with a 4-1 win over the Tampa Bay Rays yesterday.
I'm Rylan Barton.
This is NPR.
